body_paragraphs: Friday gave you a rerun of Thursday with a different star: Amazon jumped about 13% - its biggest single-day gain in over a decade - on an earnings beat, dragging the S&P up 0.7% to 7,489.72 and the Nasdaq up 1% to 25,373.85, and capping the Dow's fourth straight winning month. But the 10-year Treasury topped 4.70% for the first time since January 2025, and the 30-year hit its highest level since 2007. Two straight days now: stocks keep buying the AI trade, bonds keep pricing in something less comfortable, and neither is budging toward the other.

Yesterday's Iran 'pause' didn't survive the weekend. Kuwait's army says it intercepted a fresh wave of Iranian drones early this morning, aimed at a government facility and civilian vehicles - the attack Iran claimed Thursday and nobody had confirmed. Trump told his Cabinet at Camp David the US is planning new strikes on Iran 'as soon as this weekend.' Five months into a war that began with Ali Khamenei's assassination, only 28% of Americans approve of how he's handling it.

Closer to home: the Marlins beat the Mets 5-2 to move to 56-55, still alive for the Wild Card, while Cleveland joins Boston in calling about Otto Lopez - though the actual odds of a trade, per one insider, sit around 25% with two days left. And Miami's priciest office towers just crossed $200 a square foot for the first time, with Peter Thiel's family office paying a record $250 at 830 Brickell. If you want out of all of it tonight, tonight's rabbit hole makes the case that deep time, not headlines, is the only scale that actually explains where nuclear danger comes from - and where it might go.

themes.title: Kuwait intercepts a fresh Iranian drone wave; Trump says new US strikes are coming 'as soon as this weekend'
themes.thesis: Yesterday's ambiguous pause turns out to have been exactly that - a pause - as Kuwait confirms the attack it and the US had left unconfirmed a day earlier, and Washington signals it's about to escalate again.
themes.synthesis: Kuwait's army says it intercepted and destroyed a fresh wave of Iranian drones early Saturday, aimed at a government facility and civilian vehicles; officials call it 'Iranian aggression' and report no casualties. Separately, a tanker was hit by an unidentified projectile near the Strait of Hormuz off Oman's coast. At a Camp David Cabinet meeting, Trump said the US is planning a new wave of strikes on Iran 'as soon as this weekend,' though officials cautioned the plan could still be called off, and repeated that 'at some point, they're going to say we just can't take it anymore.' The war is five months old - it began with the February 28 assassination of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei - and only 28% of Americans approve of how Trump has handled it.

themes.why_it_matters: Thursday and Friday's 'first pause since Wednesday' framing didn't hold even one more day - a pattern worth remembering the next time this war looks like it's cooling off, and directly relevant to the oil and rate exposure running through Alex's other markets reading.

themes.title: LiDAR finds a civilization of millions hiding under the Amazon canopy
themes.thesis: The rainforest that looks like untouched wilderness turns out to be sitting on top of one of the largest ancient societies archaeology has found - proof that 'empty' is often just a failure of the instruments used to look.
themes.synthesis: Airborne laser scanning has revealed nearly 400 previously unknown earthwork sites across roughly 183,000 square kilometers of southwestern Amazonia, evidence of a multicultural civilization that flourished between 600 BCE and 850 CE and was home to millions of people. Researchers found monumental ceremonial architecture - the largest site spans 50 hectares - and extrapolate that the full territory could contain 24,000 to 30,000 such earthwork centers, far more than previously estimated. The findings, published in Nature, upend the old assumption that the pre-Columbian Amazon was too resource-poor to support large, complex societies.
themes.new_today: First dedicated coverage of the Nature LiDAR findings in this edition.
themes.why_it_matters: It's appreciation-worthy science with zero urgency attached to it - a real counterweight on a day built around a war that might restart by tomorrow, and a good prompt for how much of what looks empty is really just unmeasured.

themes.title: A single gene may decide how much a bad night's sleep costs your brain later
themes.thesis: Sleep's brain-cleaning function turns out to be genetically gated - the same lost night of sleep may matter far more for some people than others.
themes.synthesis: Researchers examined the AQP4 gene, which regulates fluid movement through the brain's glymphatic system - the overnight process that clears amyloid-beta and tau, the proteins associated with Alzheimer's. In a randomized crossover trial, normal sleep, compared with sleep deprivation, measurably increased overnight clearance of these Alzheimer's-linked biomarkers into blood plasma, and the effect appears to vary with AQP4 variants - meaning genetic risk for Alzheimer's may be amplified or dampened by sleep habits in ways specific to the individual.
themes.new_today: First dedicated coverage of the AQP4/glymphatic clearance findings in this edition.
themes.why_it_matters: It's a concrete mechanism, not just a correlation - a real answer to why 'sleep more' lands differently for different people, worth filing away against every future night that gets cut short for no good reason.

beautiful_thing.title: Vizcaya
beautiful_thing.creator: Francis Burrall Hoffman Jr. (architecture), Diego Suárez (gardens)
beautiful_thing.body: James Deering, who made his fortune running International Harvester, built Vizcaya as a winter retreat on Biscayne Bay, moving in on Christmas Day, 1916. He hired architect Francis Burrall Hoffman Jr. to design a 34-room villa modeled on an Italian Renaissance estate, the young Colombian landscape architect Diego Suárez to lay out its formal gardens, and Paul Chalfin to assemble European antiques - many centuries older than the house itself - into new compositions throughout the rooms. Deering spent his final winters there before his death in 1925; his family later conveyed the estate to Miami-Dade County, and it was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1994.

daily_puzzle.prompt: Every month, on the first Friday, an economist wakes at 8:25 a.m. to catch the jobs report land at 8:30 sharp - a ritual she's kept for a decade. This month, she sleeps straight through it, and nothing is wrong: no missed report, no career change, no broken alarm clock. Why does she get to sleep in?
daily_puzzle.hint: Not every month's first day falls on the same weekday.
daily_puzzle.solution: This month's first day is a Saturday, not a Friday - the jobs report always lands on the first Friday of the month, and this month that doesn't arrive until the following week.
daily_puzzle.explanation: 'The first Friday of the month' isn't a fixed date - it drifts depending on what weekday the month happens to start on.

timeline.summary: First tracked: nine nights of US strikes, oil up about 20% this month, 10-day ceasefire being mediated.
10-day ceasefire formally proposed; US strikes continue, Iran calls it full-scale war, Brent tops $91, war cost estimated at $37.5B.
By Wednesday, strikes reach an eleventh consecutive night; Brent pushes past $92, reviving inflation concern.

Ceasefire proposal remains unadopted; Brent closes at $94.13, a five-week high; Strait transits fall to 25 ships from a peak of 49; Saudi coalition vows a forceful response to the Houthi blockade threat.
13th consecutive night of strikes; Iran hits Kuwait and the Houthis strike two Saudi tankers; Brent crosses $100 for the first time since May; Trump considers a massive attack.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard launches a fresh drone attack on Kuwait; sirens sound across Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar; Iran rejects an Iraqi-mediated ceasefire proposal; Brent holds near $100.

US carries out no new strikes overnight for the first time since the ceasefire collapsed; an Omani delegation arrives in Tehran to discuss Strait of Hormuz shipping; Brent eases to about $96.80, down nearly 4% but still up over 12% on the week.

Iran-aligned Houthi rebels fire dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco facilities in Jizan and Yanbu, starting large fires; read as retaliation for Saudi strikes on a Houthi-held Yemeni coastal city.

The pause holds through the weekend into Monday with no new strikes reported on either front; Brent tumbles toward the mid-$80s, down roughly 7% on the session, as Trump signals openness to renewed talks with Tehran.

Trump and Netanyahu meet at the White House for the first time since the war began, calling the talks 'positive and productive' and reaffirming a shared commitment against an Iranian nuclear weapon; Brent eases further into the mid-to-high $80s.

Iran says it struck US bases in Jordan and other Gulf locations overnight; Trump vows to hit back hard and repeats a bridge-bombing threat; the US and Saudi Arabia strike Iran-backed groups in Iraq; Brent jumps back above $90.

The US launches a 'heavy wave' of new strikes on Iran; Iranian state media reports at least three civilians killed. Iran retaliates against Jordan and Kuwait, killing a worker at a Chinese-owned building in Kuwait. Trump says it is now 'our turn' to hit Iran hard.
Qatar formally condemns Iran's strikes on Jordan and Kuwait as violations of sovereignty - the first significant regional diplomatic reaction against Tehran this round.

Iran's army claims strikes on US assets at Kuwait's Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base and Bahrain's Sheikh Isa Air Base; neither government confirms it. The US conducts no fresh strikes overnight - the first pause since Wednesday's heavy wave.

Egypt reports a drone of unknown origin hit two gas vessels at its Damietta port, a possible first sign the conflict is pulling in a new country; Brent eases 1.4% to $87.78 as Hormuz tanker traffic shows tentative recovery.

Kuwait's army confirms it intercepted a fresh wave of Iranian drones aimed at a government facility and civilian vehicles, the attack Iran claimed Thursday and nobody had confirmed. A tanker is hit by an unidentified projectile near Oman.

At Camp David, Trump says the US is planning new strikes on Iran 'as soon as this weekend'; only 28% of Americans approve of his handling of the five-month-old war. Brent back above $90, WTI near $84.67.

threads.title: 2026 CRE capital markets under pressure
threads.current_state: South Florida commercial sales volume remains down 13% year over year, and the summer's biggest single industrial deal - Waste Management's $379M purchase of 146 acres in Medley - was 96% seller-financed. Rents in Miami's most sought-after office towers broke $200/sqft in July for the first time, anchored by Peter Thiel's family office paying a record $250/sqft at 830 Brickell - the most expensive office lease in county history. Q2 leasing citywide jumped nearly 45% year-over-year to 1.3 million square feet, with average asking rent readings ranging $59.66-$67.12/sqft depending on methodology, still the highest of any US market.

timeline.summary: First tracked: CBRE Q2 update shows deal volume down 24% YoY, construction spending below plan, hiring slowing.
South Florida-specific data surfaces: commercial sales volume down 13% year over year to $5.42B in H1 2026.
Waste Management pays $379M for 146 acres in Medley to build a landfill; $366M of the price, 96%, is seller financing rather than a bank loan.

A LoopNet analysis of roughly 5,000 office listings finds Miami's average asking rent, $59.66/sq ft, now the highest in the US, ahead of New York's $50.56 - a sign of how much capital has relocated to Miami since 2020 even as deal volume overall stays soft.

Pebb Capital buys a Miami Beach office building with $69M in ACORE Capital financing; a Wynwood commercial parcel sells for $24.5M, the region's priciest trade that week - real transactions behind the aggregate rent data.
Rents in Miami's top towers cross $200/sqft for the first time, anchored by Peter Thiel's family office paying a record $250/sqft at 830 Brickell; Q2 leasing citywide up nearly 45% YoY to 1.3M sq ft.

threads.title: Miami Marine Stadium's restoration referendum
threads.current_state: Miami voters decide Marine Stadium's future in an August 18 referendum (Referendum #172) on a 40-year management deal with Global Spectrum/Oak View Group and local partner Breakwater Hospitality. Under the deal, the city keeps 93% of event revenue and 85% of sponsorship income, with up to $10M toward restoration up front, followed by a separate $65-85M restoration bond. Early voting runs August 3-16; partial pile and seating repairs are already underway with county and state grant money.

timeline.summary: First tracked: City Commission approved the Global Spectrum/Oak View management deal in February; referendum set for August 18; partial restoration already underway.

Additional detail surfaces: the deal is formally Referendum #172, with early voting set for August 3-16 and a specified revenue split (93% events, 85% sponsorship) plus a separate $65-85M restoration bond beyond the initial $10M.
